decision: The one number that says the site worked
options: Share of pickup orders placed online per week
Count of site visits per week
Total online revenue per week
recommendation: Share of pickup orders placed online per week
reason: It shows whether ordering ahead is replacing walk-in hoping and phone or DM orders, which is the real problem.
question: What would tell you a customer's bread ordering has genuinely become easier than just turning up?

decision: What we measure at Place order
options: Count completed orders over started orders (checkout completion rate)
Count orders placed per day
Count abandoned carts only
recommendation: Count completed orders over started orders (checkout completion rate)
reason: It shows exactly where customers give up between choosing bread and being guaranteed a loaf.

decision: What we measure at Repeat usual loaf
options: Share of orders from customers who ordered before within 30 days
Count clicks on a reorder button
Count of new customers per week
recommendation: Share of orders from customers who ordered before within 30 days
reason: Return orders show whether people come back, and it needs only name and contact kept, not browsing history.
question: What makes someone come back to a neighbourhood bakery week after week?

label: Repeat usual loaf
reason: Return orders show whether people come back, and it needs only name and contact kept, not browsing history.
decision: What we measure at Repeat usual loaf
What we measure at Pick up bread
options: Count orders marked collected vs not collected by the baker
Count pickup-time late arrivals
Skip measuring pickup
recommendation: Count orders marked collected vs not collected by the baker
reason: Uncollected loaves are the cost to the bakery and tell us whether the pickup promise works, using one tap by the baker.

note: Data pass box by box: one measure per step, plus the single whole-page success number, keeping only what a decision would use.

decision: What happens when a loaf sells out or hits its daily limit
options: Cap each loaf per pickup day and show 'sold out' on the page
Accept all orders and let the baker sort it out
Cap each loaf and offer another pickup day when full
recommendation: Cap each loaf per pickup day and show 'sold out' on the page
reason: A guaranteed loaf is the whole promise, and a simple per-day count checked at order time prevents two people taking the last loaf.
question: What would a customer feel if they ordered a loaf and then found out it was gone?

decision: How customers get an order confirmation
options: Email confirmation with order and pickup details
Text message confirmation
On-screen confirmation only
recommendation: Email confirmation with order and pickup details
reason: Email is cheap, reliable and proven, and gives customers proof their bread is set aside.

decision: How the baker sees and receives orders
options: Simple daily order list page the baker opens, plus email on each new order
Printable list only
Orders sent to the baker's phone by text
recommendation: Simple daily order list page the baker opens, plus email on each new order
reason: A list grouped by pickup day is the plainest way for the baker to bake and pack the right amounts.

decision: Whether customers pay online or at pickup, and whether the page remembers them
options: Pay at pickup, remember name and contact on this device for a repeat usual order
Pay at pickup, no remembering
Pay online at checkout
recommendation: Pay at pickup, remember name and contact on this device for a repeat usual order
reason: No payments keeps the build small and safe, and remembering the device makes reordering a usual loaf quick.
question: What makes someone come back to the same bakery for their usual loaf week after week?

label: Repeat usual loaf
reason: No payments keeps the build small and safe, and remembering the device makes reordering a usual loaf quick.
decision: Whether customers pay online or at pickup, and whether the page remembers them

note: Engineering decisions for the bakery pre-order page: limits, failures, storage, and confirmation.

decision: Who the site serves first: regulars or new neighbours
options: Regulars who want their usual guaranteed
New customers discovering the bakery
Both equally
recommendation: Regulars who want their usual guaranteed
reason: Regulars come back for the bread and feel the sell-out pain most, so the journey is built around them first.
question: Who is the one customer who would be most upset if the bread ran out before they got there?

decision: What happens when a loaf sells out or a pickup day is full
options: Show sold out and offer another day
Allow over-ordering and let baker sort it out
Waitlist for the loaf
recommendation: Show sold out and offer another day
reason: The promise is certainty, so we never accept an order the baker cannot fill.
question: How should a customer feel when the loaf they wanted is gone?

decision: How regulars repeat their usual order
options: One tap reorder of last order on the home page
Saved favourites list
No repeat feature in v1
recommendation: One tap reorder of last order on the home page
reason: Repeat ordering is the heart of the return visit and the smallest version is a single reorder button.
question: What makes someone order the same loaf week after week?

label: Repeat usual loaf
reason: Repeat ordering is the heart of the return visit and the smallest version is a single reorder button.
decision: How regulars repeat their usual order
Cutoff and changes: how late can customers order or cancel
options: Order by evening before, cancel until cutoff
Same-day orders until a morning cutoff
No cancellation, contact the bakery
recommendation: Order by evening before, cancel until cutoff
reason: A clear cutoff lets the baker plan the bake while still letting customers fix mistakes.

note: Drafted the key journey decisions for the bakery pre-order site: who it serves first, what happens when loaves sell out, pickup-day rules, and how regulars reorder.

decision: Pay online when ordering, or pay at pickup
options: Pay at pickup
Pay online when ordering
Let customer choose either
recommendation: Pay at pickup
reason: Paying at the counter keeps the first version simple, avoids card fees and refunds, and feels like the neighbourhood bakery.
question: What would make a customer trust an order enough to turn up and collect it?

decision: What happens when a customer doesn't collect their order
options: Nothing, bread goes back on sale
Reminder, then a note on their account after repeat misses
Take a deposit up front
recommendation: Reminder, then a note on their account after repeat misses
reason: Uncollected loaves are the baker's real cost, and a gentle reminder protects them without demanding money up front.
question: How should the bakery feel when a regular forgets to pick up their bread?

decision: Cutoff and changes: how late a customer can edit or cancel an order
options: Free changes until the evening before
Free changes until baking starts, set by the baker
No changes after ordering
recommendation: Free changes until the evening before
reason: Bakers bake to the orders, so a clear cutoff protects them and tells customers exactly what they can rely on.

decision: How prices are shown and what the order total promises
options: Show each loaf's price and total, pay the same at pickup
Show prices only, bakery sets them freely
Add a pre-order fee or discount
recommendation: Show each loaf's price and total, pay the same at pickup
reason: Same price as walking in keeps ordering ahead an easy habit, and the baker can change prices later without breaking promises.

note: Worked on how customers pay for pre-ordered bread, what the bakery promises on cancellations and sell-outs, and how prices are shown.

decision: Who the first customers are: weekly regulars or occasional treat-buyers
options: Local weekly regulars
Occasional weekend treat-buyers
Both equally
recommendation: Local weekly regulars
reason: Regulars have the clearest pain (missing out on sell-outs) and the most repeat value, but we haven't confirmed this and should learn it first from the baker and a few customers.
question: Who walks into this bakery most often, and what do they usually go home disappointed about?

decision: What the order promises: guaranteed loaf set aside vs. a request the baker confirms
options: Guaranteed once placed
Baker confirms each order
Guaranteed up to a daily limit per loaf
recommendation: Guaranteed up to a daily limit per loaf
reason: Certainty is the main thing customers want, and a limit keeps the promise honest so the baker never over-commits.
question: What would make a customer trust that their loaf is truly waiting for them?

decision: How the baker sees orders to decide how much to bake
options: Simple daily totals per loaf
Full order list only
Both totals and list
recommendation: Both totals and list
reason: The 2025 small-bakery study links waste to guessing how many loaves to bake, and knowing orders ahead fixes that guess; note the paper could not be opened to verify, and it gives no figure on sell-outs or pre-order effect.

decision: What success looks like for the first few months
options: Share of regulars ordering ahead
Fewer sell-outs and less leftover bread
Orders placed per week
recommendation: Share of regulars ordering ahead
reason: It shows whether ordering is easier than just turning up, and we have no baseline numbers yet, so we'd learn the current sell-out and leftover pattern first.
question: How will you know the bakery's customers are better off because of this site?

note: Listed the four biggest decisions for the bakery pre-order site: who it serves, what the order promise is, how orders reach the baker, and what success looks like. Only the baker-visibility one rests on the single finding, whose source I could not open to verify.

decision: What ordering should feel like: quick and remembered, or guided and reassuring
options: Quick and remembered
Guided and reassuring
Quick, with a clear reassuring confirmation
recommendation: Quick, with a clear reassuring confirmation
reason: Ordering must be easier than turning up, so the path stays short (one filled button marks the main action), and the final screen gives the certainty customers came for.
question: What do your customers worry about most between deciding to order bread and walking out with it?

decision: What leads the home screen: the loaf list, or a returning customer's usual order
options: Loaf list with pickup day up top
Usual loaf first for returning customers
Same page for everyone
recommendation: Loaf list with pickup day up top
reason: Hierarchy follows the first job, picking bread for a day. A repeat shortcut (n7) sits as one secondary action until evidence says regulars need more.
question: Who orders most often, a regular with the same loaf each week or someone picking something new?

decision: What a sold-out loaf or full pickup day shows
options: Greyed loaf with a different-day link
Hide sold-out loaves
Allow orders and tell them later
recommendation: Greyed loaf with a different-day link
reason: Showing the empty state plainly with a next step builds trust and avoids false promises, and sell-outs are the frustration this site exists to fix.
question: When bread has sold out before, what did customers do next, and how did it feel?

decision: Which single accent colour and type pairing gives a warm neighbourhood feel
options: Warm crust-brown accent, serif display, sans text
Wheat-yellow accent, rounded display, sans text
Neutral only, no accent
recommendation: Warm crust-brown accent, serif display, sans text
reason: One accent on 90 to 95% neutral paper and near-ink, two faces with fixed jobs, no violet; this reads as a local bakery rather than a tech product.
